vignette:
Fatima, a 77-year-old tutor living alone in a quiet American suburb, had spent much of her life teaching in a city that became a war zone. The event that shattered her happened while she was conducting a small class: a mortar shell struck the building next door, and through the dust and screaming she had to shepherd her students out a narrow back exit. The terror of that moment—the crush of bodies, the thought that she might not make it—never left her. Now, when she remembers it, she feels the same terror pressing in, and sometimes, without any warning, a sudden sound or a crowded hallway will bring the full memory back, vivid and as if it is happening right now.

Fatima has come to believe that she is weak. The thought that she cannot handle the memory, that if she lets herself think about it she will fall apart, has become a fixed idea. This conviction that she was weak and could not cope kept her mind circling back to the moment of the explosion, as if she needed to re‑witness exactly where she had been lost, each return sharpening the memory rather than dulling it. This belief drives much of what she does. She has taken to always sitting near the door when she tutors, and she scans the room for the exit before she can focus on her student’s work. She avoids the news—television programmes, films, even passing headlines about conflict—because she is certain that exposure will trigger the collapse she fears. And she catches herself dwelling on how she used to be before the event, on the capable woman who did not need to check where the door was. In these moments, she feels dead inside, hollowed out by the contrast.

Her strategies, however, have only deepened the problem. By staying near the exit, she never gives her mind a chance to learn that she is safe—instead, the vigilance itself keeps the traumatic scene alive. Avoiding media means she has no practice processing reminders, so when an unexpected cue does break through, the memory hits with undiminished force, the terror as fresh as the day it happened. And dwelling on her former self reinforces the belief that she is now a broken person; each time she compares, she feels weaker, more numb. The logic of her avoidance is airtight to her, yet the loops tighten with every passing week.

She still tutors, but she now chooses only students who come to her home, and she insists that the chair she uses be the one closest to the front door. She has stopped taking new clients if their schedule would require her to sit in a different room. A colleague once asked why she always sat by the exit, and Fatima made an excuse about back pain. She could not say the real reason—that talking about it feels like stepping off a cliff. What frightens her most is the thought that one day a door will be blocked, or a student will mention a war film, and she will lose control in front of someone. She came to therapy because a neighbour noticed she was withdrawing and gently insisted that she needed help. Fatima does not know if she can be helped, but she knows she cannot go on living this way, scanning every room for a way out.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not show a causal relationship where negative appraisals (e.g., belief she is weak or will fall apart) drive or influence the memory. Instead, the memory triggers appraisals, and appraisals lead to maladaptive strategies, which in turn affect the memory.
